children.heading: Abstract

content.text: The problem of an optimal mapping between Hilbert spaces *IN* and *OUT*, based on a series of density matrix mapping measurements ρ(l)→ϱ(l)\rho^{(l)}\to\varrho^{(l)}, l=1​…​Ml=1\dots M, is formulated as an optimization problem maximizing the total fidelity ℱ=∑l=1Mω(l)​F​(ϱ(l),∑sBs​ρ(l)​Bs†)\mathcal{F}=\sum\_{l=1}^{M}\omega^{(l)}F\left(\varrho^{(l)},\sum\_{s}B\_{s}\rho^{(l)}B^{\dagger}\_{s}\right) subject to probability preservation constraints on Kraus operators BsB\_{s}. For F⁡(ϱ,σ)F(\varrho,\sigma) in the form that total fidelity can be represented as a quadratic form with superoperator ℱ=∑s⟨Bs|S|Bs⟩\mathcal{F}=\sum\_{s}\left\langle B\_{s}\middle|S\middle|B\_{s}\right\rangle (either exactly or as an approximation) an iterative algorithm is developed. The work introduces two important generalizations of unitary learning: 1. *IN*/*OUT* states are represented as density matrices. 2. The mapping itself is formulated as a mixed unitary quantum channel A​O​U​T=∑s|ws|2​𝒰s​A​I​N​𝒰s†A^{\emph{OUT}}=\sum\_{s}|w\_{s}|^{2}\mathcal{U}\_{s}A^{\emph{IN}}\mathcal{U}\_{s}^{\dagger} (no general quantum channel yet). This marks a crucial advancement from the commonly studied unitary mapping of pure states ϕl=𝒰​ψl\phi\_{l}=\mathcal{U}\psi\_{l} to a quantum channel, what allows us to distinguish probabilistic mixture of states and their superposition. An application of the approach is demonstrated on unitary learning of density matrix mapping ϱ(l)=𝒰​ρ(l)​𝒰†\varrho^{(l)}=\mathcal{U}\rho^{(l)}\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}, in this case a quadratic on 𝒰\mathcal{U} fidelity can be constructed by considering ρ(l)→ϱ(l)\sqrt{\rho^{(l)}}\to\sqrt{\varrho^{(l)}} mapping, and on a quantum channel, where quadratic on BsB\_{s} fidelity is an approximation — a quantum channel is then obtained as a hierarchy of unitary mappings, a mixed unitary channel. The approach can be applied to studying quantum inverse problems, variational quantum algorithms, quantum tomography, and more. A software product implementing the algorithm [is available](http://www.ioffe.ru/LNEPS/malyshkin/code_polynomials_quadratures.zip) from the authors.
Dedicated to the memory of Ivan Anatol’evich Komarchev

children.heading: I Introduction

content.text: The form of knowledge representation stands out as a crucial and distinctive feature in any approach to Machine Learning (ML). The utilization of unitary operators for knowledge representation has garnered increasing attention recently[Bisio et al. 2010](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib1); [Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2); [Hyland and Rätsch 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib3). In nature most of dynamic equations are equivalent to a sequence of infinitesimal unitary transformations: Newton, Maxwell, Schrödinger equations. This inherent connection with unitary transformations makes it particularly appealing to represent knowledge in this form. Most of the existing works consider algorithms that take wavefunction as input and construct a unitary operator providing a high value of mapping fidelity[Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2); [Hyland and Rätsch 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib3); [Lloyd and Maity 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib4); they are mostly different in parametrization of unitary operator [Raza 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib5) and optimization details. Such a pure state to pure state mapping is a limited form of quantum evolution. There are a few works[Pai et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib6); [Huang et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib7); [González et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib8); [Yu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib9) that consider unitary learning with density matrix input. Real systems probability should be described by a mixed state (density matrix) what allows to distinguish probabilistic mixture of states and their superposition. There are two sources of mixed states: 1. The input data itself can be in mixed state. 2. ​I​N→​O​U​T\emph{IN}\to\emph{OUT} mapping of a general quantum channel can transform a pure state input into a mixed state output. Unitary mapping is a simple example of a quantum channel converting a pure state into a pure state.

In our previous works[Malyshkin 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib10); [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) the quantum mechanics inverse problem of optimal unitary mapping of pure states was converted to a [QCQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratically_constrained_quadratic_program) (Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program) problem, a novel algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) was formulated, and an efficient iterative global optimization algorithm was developed. This algorithm can be applied to quantum inverse problems, variational quantum algorithms [Cerezo et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib12); [Park and Killoran 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib13); [Wang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib14) with a cost function in the form C⁡(θ)=Tr​O​𝒰​(θ)​ρ0​𝒰†​(θ)C(\theta)=\mathrm{Tr}\,O\mathcal{U}(\theta)\rho\_{0}\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}(\theta), quantum tomography[D’Ariano et al. 2003](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib15); [Lvovsky and Raymer 2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib16); [Torlai et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib17); [Ahmed et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib18), various classical problems, and many others. We do not have a formal proof of the developed algorithm’s convergence, but among the millions of test runs, only a few did not converge to the global maximum. This could possibly be caused by numerical instability. In the current work, we generalize our algorithm to mixed states and further extend it to quantum channels. This generalization is possible as long as the total fidelity can be represented as a quadratic form on quantum channel mapping operators.

In the case of unitary mapping (D=nD=n, Ns=1N\_{s}=1) of mixed states there are several good choices for fidelity, for example a quantum channel mapping the square root of density matrix ρ→ϱ\sqrt{\rho}\to\sqrt{\varrho} with a unitary operator ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), it provides the exact fidelity as a quadratic form. Together with the available iterative algorithm, this problem may be considered mostly solved.

In the case of a general quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) constructing fidelity as the quadratic form of Eq. ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) on quantum channel mapping operators can be challenging. We have developed several approximations that can be used with the iterative algorithm and have constructed a hierarchy of mapping operators ([52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E52 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) as a mixed unitary channel. A demonstration of several approximations is presented in Section [IV.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.SS1 "IV.1 A Demonstration of Constructed Hierarchy of Operators ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). The problem of finding a good quadratic (on mapping operators) fidelity for Kraus rank Ns>1N\_{s}>1 quantum channels requires more research and is related to a physical meaning of quantum channel mapping. Even when fidelity is expressed as the quadratic form of Eq. ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), we currently only have a numerical algorithm to approximate the data using a mixed unitary channel. A general reconstruction of quantum channels is not yet available.

The paper is organized as follows. After formulating the problem, the unitary mapping of mixed states is considered in Section [III](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3 "III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). Section [IV](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4 "IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") focuses on the construction of a hierarchy of unitary operators. In the conclusion, we discuss the results obtained for the problem of quantum channel reconstruction. Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") provides a detailed description of the numerical solution that uses algebraic techniques. Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2 "Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") presents a generalization of the novel algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) to the nonstationary case and introduces a time-dependent Schrödinger-like equation for unitary operator dynamics ([87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E87 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3 "Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") explores potential generalizations to states with memory, while Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A4 "Appendix D An estimate of computational complexity ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") estimates the algorithm’s computational complexity.

This paper is accompanied by a software which [is available](http://www.ioffe.ru/LNEPS/malyshkin/code_polynomials_quadratures.zip) from Ref. [Malyshkin 2014](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib19); all references to code in the paper correspond to this software.

children.heading: II Formulation of the Problem

content.text: In [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11), we considered data of vector-to-vector pure state mapping, l=1​…​Ml=1\dots M,

The weights ω(l)\omega^{(l)} are typically all equal to 1.11 1 Some authors use ω(l)=1/M\omega^{(l)}=1/M to normalize the fidelity to the range [0:1][0:1]. However, this approach is inconvenient because ℱ\mathcal{F} is no longer an [extensive quantity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intensive_and_extensive_properties) in the sense that, for two sets of observations, the total fidelity is no longer the sum of the two — losing its additive property. For this reason, normalizing to the number of observations is preferred over normalizing to [0:1][0:1]. However, they can be set to different values if the observations are made with different accuracy, this is particularly convenient for classical systems. The usefulness of ω(l)\omega^{(l)} weights also arises in models that comprise a number of identical mappings; in this case one may consider only distinct mappings and set ω(l)\omega^{(l)} equal to the number of times the observation was encountered in the sample. The problem of maximizing total fidelity

was considered, and a numerical algorithm finding the global maximum of ℱ\mathcal{F} was developed. Found solution 𝒰\mathcal{U}, a partially unitary matrix of dim(​O​U​T)×dim(​I​N)\dim(\emph{OUT})\times\dim(\emph{IN}) (D×nD\times n)

converts any operator between two Hilbert spaces, for example it converts a pure state A​I​N=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|A^{\emph{IN}}=\Ket{\psi}\Bra{\psi} into a pure state A​O​U​T=|𝒰|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|𝒰†|A^{\emph{OUT}}=\Ket{\mathcal{U}|\psi}\Bra{\psi|\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}}. For D=nD=n it is a trace preserving map, and for D<nD<n it is a [trace decreasing map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_channel) quantum channel. The input data ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) represent pure state to pure state mapping. This type of mapping is not the most general, it cannot describe systems with effects like [quantum decoherence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_decoherence). For example a simple [Markov chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain) system converts a pure state |ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\Ket{\psi}\Bra{\psi} into a density matrix state, see Appendix I of Ref. [Malyshkin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib20).

In this work a more general mapping between Hilbert spaces *IN* of |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} (dimension nn) and *OUT* of |ϕ⟩\Ket{\phi} (dimension DD) is considered. [Kraus’ theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_operation#Kraus_operators) determines the most general form of mapping between Hilbert spaces[Jamiołkowski 1972](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib21); [Kraus 1983](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib22); [Joos et al. 2013](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib23):

the number of terms in the sum NsN\_{s} is called the Kraus rank, see Choi’s theorem [Choi 1975](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib24) and Belavkin’s Radon-Nikodym theorem for completely positive maps [Belavkin and Staszewski 1986](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib25). The Kraus operators BsB\_{s} satisfy the constraints that unit A​I​NA^{\emph{IN}} is converted to unit A​O​U​TA^{\emph{OUT}}. There are other options to construct a quantum channel, in [Malyshkin 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib10); [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) we considered a quantum channel that transforms the Gram matrix in space |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} into the Gram matrix in space |ϕ⟩\Ket{\phi}; with proper regularization it can be reduced to the same form.

We further generalize Kraus operators BsB\_{s} by considering them to be rectangular D×nD\times n matrices instead of being limited to Hilbert space mapping into itself. The term “partially Kraus” is used in the same sense as “partially unitary” — we consider rectangular matrices D≤nD\leq n mapping Hilbert spaces of different dimensions.22 2 Here, instead of the usual constraint ∑s=0Ns−1Bs†​Bs=𝟙\sum\_{s=0}^{N\_{s}-1}B\_{s}^{\dagger}B\_{s}=\mathds{1} ([55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E55 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) we use the constraint ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E5 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) to fully utilize our numerical algorithm in the case of Ns=1N\_{s}=1. Constraint ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E5 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) imposes D⁡(D+1)/2D(D+1)/2 independent conditions, whereas constraint ([55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E55 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) imposes n⁡(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2 independent conditions. When D=nD=n both definitions coincide. However, for Ns=1N\_{s}=1 and D<nD<n, the constraint ([55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E55 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) fails to satisfy the minimal Kraus rank condition ([56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E56 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), but the constraints ([5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E5 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) are applicable in the numerical study of trace-decreasing maps when Ns=1N\_{s}=1 and D<nD<n. Additionally, the Lagrange multiplier calculation method described in Appendix [A.4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS4 "A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"), along with the convergence-helper constraints in Appendix [A.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS5 "A.5 Convergence-Helper Linear Constraints ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"), facilitates the incorporation of quadratic form constraints of any type. For D<nD<n a partially unitary quantum channel ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) does not preserve the density matrix trace. For a large enough NsN\_{s}, as in the condition ([56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E56 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), the form of Eq. ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) allows us to construct a trace preserving quantum channel, for example to implement an operation of [partial trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_trace).

Kraus operators selection is not unique. In addition to the familiar exp⁡(i​φ)\exp(i\varphi) phase factor (±1\pm 1 for real space), there is a [gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_theory) that regulates redundant degrees of freedom. The most well-known is the canonical form:

However, other gauges can be used. See Appendix [A.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS1 "A.1 Transforming Kraus Operators to Canonical Form ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") for an algorithm transforming Kraus operators to canonical form.

Back in [Malyshkin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib20); [Malyshkin 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib10) we considered, instead of ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), the data of density matrix to density matrix mapping ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) — just replace Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} from ([19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E19 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) by ([18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E18 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) or ([30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E30 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Whereas input/output data in density matrix form distinguishes probabilistic mixture of states and their superposition, the transform ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) cannot map such data exactly, it has insufficient expressive power. Only a general quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) mapping has sufficient expressive power to construct learning models from general data, for example with a decoherence effect, or a much more seldom but very interesting effects of pure state formation from mixed state input — spontaneous coherence, exhibited in entropy decrease, synchronizing, coherent responses of (ψA+ψB)2≫ψA2+ψB2\left(\psi\_{A}+\psi\_{B}\right)^{2}\gg\psi^{2}\_{A}+\psi^{2}\_{B} type, etc.

The ρ(l)\rho^{(l)} is a measured Hermitian density matrix n×nn\times n in the |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} space, while the ϱ(l)\varrho^{(l)} is a measured Hermitian density matrix D×DD\times D in the |ϕ⟩\Ket{\phi} space. Both ρ\rho and ϱ\varrho density operators are Hermitian matrices with positive eigenvalues and having unit [trace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trace_(linear_algebra)) (the sum of diagonal elements). Previously considered data ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) corresponded to ρ(l)=|ψl⟩​⟨ψl|\rho^{(l)}=\Ket{\psi\_{l}}\Bra{\psi\_{l}} and ϱ(l)=|ϕl⟩​⟨ϕl|\varrho^{(l)}=\Ket{\phi\_{l}}\Bra{\phi\_{l}}. The optimization problem becomes
where σ=AO​U​T\sigma=A^{OUT} and ρ=AI​N\rho=A^{IN} — the σ\sigma is the ρ\rho passed through the quantum channel.

It should be noted that while for wavefunction mapping ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), in the seldom case of a classic system with known wavefunctions phases, a regression type technique is sometimes applicable, for density matrix mapping ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), which is always quadratic on 𝒰\mathcal{U} ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), no regression can possibly be applied.

We need to define the total fidelity ℱ\mathcal{F} of the ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) transform, which is a sum of contributions from all MM observations. For each observation of the *IN* to *OUT* mapping, an accuracy factor FF ranging [0:1][0:1] should be defined. For the theory presented in this paper to be applicable, this factor must be quadratic with respect to the operator 𝒰\mathcal{U} (an instance of BsB\_{s}). For pure state to pure state mapping ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) it is a squared projection, the [fidelity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidelity_of_quantum_states)
For mixed state mapping ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) a similar expression

is bounded between 00 and Tr​ϱ2≤1\mathrm{Tr}\varrho^{2}\leq 1, it has the meaning of a measured probability of probability that reaches the maximal value 11 only in pure states. A standard definition of fidelity between mixed states ϱ,σ\varrho,\sigma, [Nielsen and Chuang 2010](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib26) p. 409, [Wilde 2011](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib27) p. 285,

creates calculation difficulties since it requires taking matrix square root of an expression with BsB\_{s} sum, and it is not explicitly quadratic. There is an option to use a quality criterion based on the conditional entropy of O​U​T|I​NOUT|IN states [Jenčová 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib28). In the general case, this requires a joint density matrix ρ⁡(O​U​T,I​N)\rho(OUT,IN) [Levitin 1999](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib29). The tensor Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} ([18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E18 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) can be viewed as a joint density matrix ρ⁡(O​U​T,I​N)\rho(OUT,IN) averaged over MM observations in the sample. However, in the case where Ns>1N\_{s}>1, we were unable to express the conditional entropy in quadratic form with respect to BsB\_{s}, and we will leave this aspect of conditional entropy as a quality criterion for future research. In the Ns=1N\_{s}=1 case, the Kullback-Leibler divergence (Eq. [32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E32 "In III.1 A Conditional Entropy Based Similarity ‣ III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) can be directly applied.

i.e. the L2L^{2} of a vector obtained from all D2D^{2} matrix elements of ϱ\varrho gives the trace of ϱ2\varrho^{2}. This provides a closeness criterion, FcF^{c}, which acts as a “correlation” between the density matrices ϱi​j\varrho\_{ij} and σi​j\sigma\_{ij}, treated as if they were vectors.

It can be viewed as Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma} ([10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E10 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) with an adjusted contribution for mixed states. The practical issue with it is that σ\sigma, in the denominator, depends on the quantum channel operators BsB\_{s}; to obtain a workable expression, one can replace the σ\sigma-normalized denominator by the input density matrix ρ\rho

Here, the entity denoted as σ⁡(ρ)\sigma(\rho) is obtained by passing ρ\rho through the quantum channel using either the transformation in ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) or ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Since σ\sigma does not appear in the denominator, Eq. ([14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E14 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) is quadratic in the quantum channel mapping operators. This expression uses ([12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E12 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and treats density matrices as if they were vectors. It is linear in σ\sigma and quadratic in 𝒰\mathcal{U}; for unitary mapping (D=nD=n, Ns=1N\_{s}=1), we have Tr​ρ2=Tr​σ2\mathrm{Tr}\rho^{2}=\mathrm{Tr}\sigma^{2}, and thus FvF^{v} matches FcF^{c}. The Fp​r​o​pF^{prop} is not such a function, which makes it problematic to use. A simple Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma} as density matrices trace ([10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E10 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) is a quadratic function, but it is not normalized for Nr>1N\_{r}>1 or Ns>1N\_{s}>1: it produces the exact result only for pure state input (Nr=1N\_{r}=1) and unitary (Ns=1N\_{s}=1) mappings, see Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ III.2 A Demonstration Of Density Matrix Square Root Mapping ‣ III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")a. The mapping ρk​k′(l)→ϱj​j′(l)\sqrt{\rho^{(l)}\_{kk^{\prime}}}\to\sqrt{\varrho^{(l)}\_{jj^{\prime}}} allows us to introduce Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} ([31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E31 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) considering ϱ\sqrt{\varrho} and ρ\sqrt{\rho} as if they were actually measured density operators ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). In the unitary case Ns=1N\_{s}=1 it produces the correct value ℱ=M\mathcal{F}=M for any rank of the input density matrix ρ\rho, this is an important result of this work. In this Ns=1N\_{s}=1 case for each NrN\_{r} we also run the operator 𝒰\mathcal{U} reconstruction algorithm of Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") — it is correctly (with zero error) recovered (up to a sign) for any NrN\_{r} and any measure of closeness used: Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma}, FvF^{v}, FN​ϱ2F^{N\varrho^{2}}, or Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}}, regardless of the specifics of FF. This occurs only for exact mapping; when a noise is present in the data — the low values of Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma} make it problematic to reconstruct the quantum channel from input density matrices. The Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} does not have this limitation as for Ns=1N\_{s}=1 it is equal to proper fidelity Fp​r​o​pF^{prop} ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E11 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). We see Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} as a very promising approach to the problem of reconstructing a unitary operator from a set of mixed states density matrix mapping. Another one if FvF^{v} ([14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E14 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), which treats density matrices as “vectors”, but it does not have a clear physical meaning.

The situation with quantum channels of Kraus rank Ns>1N\_{s}>1 is more problematic. The Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma} strongly underestimates the fidelity, and the Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} is no longer correct because when there is more than one term in the sum of ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), no quantum channel simultaneously converts ρ\rho and ρ\sqrt{\rho} between Hilbert spaces. The main problem we encountered is constructing a fidelity that can be expressed as a quadratic function of BsB\_{s} in the form of ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Not every fidelity can be expressed in this form. Using a proxy, such as Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma}, FN​ϱ2F^{N\varrho^{2}}, etc., creates difficulties – for example it may become possible to obtain a fidelity value greater than the one calculated with the exact mapping of the quantum channel. This is the main requirement for a “fidelity proxy”: it should reach the maximal value at the exact mapping of the quantum channel, see Section [IV.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.SS1 "IV.1 A Demonstration of Constructed Hierarchy of Operators ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") below for counterexamples.

children.heading: IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators

content.text: As discussed below in Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"), a direct numerical attempt to obtain Kraus operators ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) in canonical gauge ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) does not work due to the degeneracy caused by the increased eigenproblem dimension from D​nDn to Ns​D​nN\_{s}Dn and the difficulty in formulating convergence helper constraints. We previously attempted to use a completely different approach for finding Kraus operators that involved a special parametrization of operators. However, it turned out to be not very stable numerically and applicable only to problems of small dimensions, n≲3n\lesssim 3, such as [SO(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_rotation_group), see [Schäfers et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib38) for a similar consideration.

Let us approach the problem of quantum channel reconstruction from a “numerical algorithm” perspective. What quantum channel problem we can efficiently solve for high dimension, i.e. D≤n>50D\leq n>50? Actually — only the problem of finding the optimal unitary mapping ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) that maximizes ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) subject to partial unitarity constraints ([28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E28 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

Our algorithm [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) has good stability and convergence. For an updated version see Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") and set Ns=1N\_{s}=1 in all formulas. Now, instead of optimizing the Kraus problem ([23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E23 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) subject to constraints ([24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E24 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), consider the unitary hierarchy. A quantum channel is built as55 5 This quantum channel has an interesting physical interpretation. If ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) represents a time evolution, then one may think of it as a quantum system evolving with several Hamiltonians at once, 𝒰[s]=exp⁡[−i​tℏ​Hs]\mathcal{U}^{[s]}=\exp\left[-i\frac{t}{\hbar}H\_{s}\right], rather than as a system evolving with the single Hamiltonian H=∑sHsH=\sum\limits\_{s}H\_{s}.

Since the weights are positive, the channel is a convex combination of unitary channels — a [mixed unitary channel](https://learning.quantum.ibm.com/course/general-formulation-of-quantum-information/quantum-channels#convex-combinations-of-channels). Note that not every quantum channel can be represented as a mixed-unitary channel[Lee and Watrous 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib39). It may look as the sum ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) exactly represents the Kraus quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) with Bs=ws​𝒰[s]B\_{s}=w\_{s}\mathcal{U}^{[s]} (they are not necessary in the canonical form ([6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E6 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), see Appendix [A.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS1 "A.1 Transforming Kraus Operators to Canonical Form ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") for a transformation), but actual Kraus rank can be lower than the number of terms in the sum ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Considering this convex combination of unitary channels we can solve the problem incrementally. This is the cost required to apply our numerical method[Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) to quantum channel reconstruction.

By continuously solving (s=0,1,2,…s=0,1,2,\dots) the optimization problem ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) subject to the constraints ([28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E28 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E45 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) we can build the required hierarchy of solutions (λi​j[s],uj​k[s])\left(\lambda^{[s]}\_{ij},u^{[s]}\_{jk}\right) to reconstruct the quantum channel from it, see com/polytechnik/kgo/KGOHierarchy.java for an implementation. The obtained hierarchy may have up to D​nDn solutions, which is the maximum possible number NsN\_{s} of terms in the Kraus sum ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

An application of the constructed hierarchy typically occurs when a nonunitary operator 𝒱\mathcal{V} is available that provides a high value of fidelity. An example of such an operator can be a solution to the optimization problem ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) subject to partial constraints (Eq. ([26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E26 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) with Ns=1N\_{s}=1), which does not satisfy the full set of constraints ([28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E28 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The expansion ([48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E48 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) allows constructing a mixed unitary channel that provides a similar value of fidelity. The problem of constructing a quantum channel is reduced to two steps: 1. Find a nonunitary operator to estimate the maximum possible fidelity, and then 2. Find a mixed unitary channel that gives approximately the same fidelity. This approach allows us to consider a sequence of Ns=1N\_{s}=1 problems instead of a single problem with a high Kraus rank NsN\_{s}. The only factor that limits this program is the formulation of the actual objective function as a quadratic form on quantum channel operators. In most cases, this is possible only through some kind of approximation, which significantly limits its applicability.

children.heading: IV.1 A Demonstration of Constructed Hierarchy of Operators

content.text: Let us demonstrate the construction of operators hierarchy. First, we would like to mention that this problem is more difficult for numerical solution than the original ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). With the “external” constraints ([45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E45 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) added, we were able to solve the problem with NsN\_{s} not greater than 55 to 1010, depending on the values of DD and nn. The first difficulty arises from numerical instability and the need for a new [adjustment algorithm](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E73 "In A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") to satisfy both the ([28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E28 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E45 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) constraints, however this problem is technical and can be resolved with a little effort. The second difficulty is a significant one. The optimization problem we are able to solve is a quadratic functional ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) optimization. However, mixed states fidelity ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E11 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) is not of this form, thus it cannot be directly applied to a general quantum channel. In the unitary case where Ns=1N\_{s}=1, there are several good options, the most noticeable being Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} ([31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E31 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). In cases where Ns>1N\_{s}>1, there are no good options, as depicted in Fig.[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ III.2 A Demonstration Of Density Matrix Square Root Mapping ‣ III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")b. For this reason we try a number of “proxies” for total fidelity ([8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E8 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Specifically Fϱ​σF^{\varrho\sigma} ([10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E10 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), FvF^{v} ([14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E14 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), FN​ϱ2F^{N\varrho^{2}} ([15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E15 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and Fϱ​ρF^{\sqrt{\varrho}\sqrt{\rho}} ([31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E31 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). These four expressions are quadratic in 𝒰\mathcal{U} what allows us to build a Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} to which the optimization technique can be applied.

Consider a demonstration. We generate a quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) of dimension D=n=10D=n=10 with Kraus rank Ns=3N\_{s}=3. children.heading: V Conclusion

content.text: We construct “quantum mechanics over quantum mechanics” by generalizing eigenstates to quantum channel mapping operators. While in traditional quantum mechanics the stationary Schrödinger equation determines system eigenstates, in our approach the algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) determines quantum channel mapping operators. The total fidelity must be a quadratic function on operators ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) for the problem to be represented in the form ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

The technique was applied to the unitary mapping of density matrices. Since, for unitary mapping, the same quantum channel converts both the density matrix and its square root, the most promising approach is to convert the density matrix mapping ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) to the density matrix square root mapping ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), to which we can apply our QCQP optimization algorithm. This allows us to employ unitary learning in the application to density matrix mapping, representing an important advancement from the commonly studied unitary mapping of pure states ϕl=𝒰​ψl\phi\_{l}=\mathcal{U}\psi\_{l}; it allows us to distinguish between a probabilistic mixture of states and their superposition. The technique was tested on a number of randomly generated density matrices ρ(l)\rho^{(l)} of different ranks unitary mapped to ϱ(l)\varrho^{(l)}; in all cases the unitary quantum channel ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) was perfectly recovered.

The problem was then generalized to quantum channels ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) with Kraus rank Ns>1N\_{s}>1. Reconstructing a general quantum channel mapping appears to be significantly more challenging. First, we were unable to represent the proper fidelity ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E11 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) as a quadratic form of the mapping operators, necessitating the use of approximations discussed in Section [II](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2 "II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). Developing a better quadratic fidelity representation (for mapping operators) is a subject for future research and is closely tied to the physical interpretation of quantum channels. Second, even when an approximate quadratic form for fidelity is obtained, the algorithm described in Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") fails to converge for Ns>1N\_{s}>1. We expect, however, that implementing advanced constraint methods could lead to improvements. If, instead of reconstructing an arbitrary quantum channel, we restrict the problem to constructing a mixed unitary channel ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) using a hierarchy of unitary operators, then the problem becomes solvable, as detailed in Section [IV](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4 "IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). The results, however, are less satisfactory than desired due to a “double approximation”: first, approximating fidelity with a quadratic form, and second, relying on a mixed unitary quantum channel instead of a general one.

In this work, we have studied quantum channels that convert: a unit matrix from *IN* to *OUT* (standard definition), a Gram matrix from *IN* to *OUT*, and a ρ\sqrt{\rho} to ϱ\sqrt{\varrho}. We developed a method for finding the global maximum by solving a novel algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), see Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2 "Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"), which presents a generalization of this algebraic problem to the nonstationary case and introduces a time-dependent Schrödinger-like equation for operator 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t). We anticipate that applying memoryless quantum channel mappings to other problems could provide a solid foundation for a new form of machine learning knowledge representation. For initial insights into quantum channels with memory, see Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3 "Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") below.

* • The ability to simultaneously include quadratic constraints of different types, such as ([24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E24 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), or alternatively, ([54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E54 "In IV.2 Trace Preserving Maps ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), requires the introduction of two kinds of Lagrange multipliers: λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′\nu\_{ss^{\prime}}. children.heading: A.1 Transforming Kraus Operators to Canonical Form

content.text: The selection of Kraus operators BsB\_{s} in which to evaluate ([23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E23 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) is nonunique, there should be a gauge that regulates redundant degrees of freedom. For example consider data of exact unitary mapping |ψl⟩​⟨ψl|→|ϕl⟩​⟨ϕl|\Ket{\psi\_{l}}\Bra{\psi\_{l}}\to\Ket{\phi\_{l}}\Bra{\phi\_{l}} with an operator 𝒰\mathcal{U} providing perfect coverage in ([2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E2 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Let we want to describe this data with ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) mapping of Kraus rank Ns=2N\_{s}=2. Then any combination Bs=ws​𝒰B\_{s}=w\_{s}\mathcal{U} with 1=∑s|ws|21=\sum\_{s}|w\_{s}|^{2} is a solution. The problem becomes degenerate. This creates difficulty in both analyzing the results and achieving convergence in the iterative algorithm – any degeneracy greatly degrades it. It is common to consider Kraus operators BsB\_{s} in the canonical form ([6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E6 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The problem becomes: converting a given bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} matrix to the canonical form of Eq. ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

Kraus operators can be considered as some superoperator states, similar to density matrix states, but ket |⋅⟩\Ket{\cdot} and bra ⟨⋅|\Bra{\cdot} are now operators: ∑s|Bs⟩​⟨Bs|\sum\_{s}\Ket{B\_{s}}\Bra{B\_{s}}, not vectors. This algebra can be uses in the expansion of tensors, such as Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} ([49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E49 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) — then evaluating ℱ\mathcal{F} is an inner product of superoperators. In this work we are not going to discuss the construction of superoperators algebra and its applications. The most important application is the construction of operators hierarchy in Section [IV](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4 "IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"), what allows us to reconstruct a quantum channel from observable data. There are a number of other interesting features that arise on this path and we hope to present a detailed discussion elsewhere. In this appendix we limit ourselves to one small but important problem.

Assume we obtained a partially Kraus operator in the form of a matrix bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} that evaluates the fidelity to some ℱ\mathcal{F} ([23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E23 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The problem is to convert bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} to a new b~s,j​k\widetilde{b}\_{s,jk} satisfying the ([25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E25 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) while maintaining the same value of the functional ℱ\mathcal{F}. The solution is not unique and requires a gauge, akin to basis orthogonalization. Since the tensor Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} does not depend on the Kraus index ss, a solution can be readily found. We use the same technique previously employed in adjusting for partial unitarity[Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11), as outlined in Appendix [A.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS2 "A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). content.text: The variation of the Lagrangian ℒ\mathcal{L} ([57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E57 "In Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) must be zero in the iteration state bs,j​kb\_{s,jk}

There are a total of Ns​D​nN\_{s}Dn equations. They are all satisfied if bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} is extremal in ([59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E59 "In Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} used, however, has the orthogonality adjustment procedure of Appendix [A.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS2 "A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") applied to it and the Lagrangian variation is no longer zero. Lagrange multipliers are Hermitian matrices λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}}, they have D⁡(D+1)/2D(D+1)/2 and Ns​(Ns−1)/2N\_{s}(N\_{s}-1)/2 independent values thus all the Ns​D​nN\_{s}Dn equations cannot be simultaneously satisfied. We need to select the λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}} to ensure they best satisfy the zero variation condition for a given bs,j​kb\_{s,jk}. Consider the L2L^{2} norm of ([80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E80 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and find the λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}} minimizing the sum of squares.

To simplify the minimization of ([81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E81 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) it is convenient to map λi​j\lambda\_{ij} into a vector of independent components λr\lambda\_{r}. One can note that for j≤ij\leq i the vector index can be taken as r=i⁡(i+1)/2+jr=i(i+1)/2+j (if j>ij>i swap them). Similarly for νr
u\_{r} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}} take the vector index as r=s⁡(s−1)/2+s′r=s(s-1)/2+s^{\prime} for s′<ss^{\prime}<s otherwise swap the indexes. Then differentiate ([81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E81 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) over λr\lambda\_{r} and νr
u\_{r} to obtain a linear system with respect to them. Back in [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) a similar linear system was analytically solved and an explicit expression for λi​j\lambda\_{ij} was obtained.

This is an analytic solution in the case Ns=1N\_{s}=1 with uj​k=b0,j​ku\_{jk}=b\_{0,jk} satisfying the ([28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E28 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) constraints, see com/polytechnik/kgo/LagrangeMultipliersPartialSubspace.java:calculateRegularLambda for an implementation of this special case. In the general case we have two types of Lagrange multipliers: λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}}, which prevents us from obtaining an analytic solution. But the problem is straightforward: take each term from ([80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E80 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), square it, and sum over all s,i,qs,i,q. Differentiate this sum of squares with respect to the vectors λr\lambda\_{r} and νr
u\_{r} to obtain a linear system, then solve it. The calculations are straightforward but lengthy, see com/polytechnik/kgo/LagrangeMultipliersNaiveKraus.java:getLagrangeMultipliers for an implementation that, given bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} and Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}}, calculates the Lagrange multiplier matrices λi​j\lambda\_{ij} and νs​s′
u\_{ss^{\prime}}.

This approach differs from the commonly used one in that we only utilize the Lagrangian variation ([80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E80 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) to calculate Lagrange multipliers. The bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} is then determined from the eigenproblem solution with these Lagrange multipliers used in ([58](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E58 "In Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). This allows us to apply constraint satisfying adjustments to the bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} before using it in the calculation of Lagrange multipliers. We cannot simultaneously solve the optimization problem for Lagrange multipliers λi​j\lambda\_{ij}, νs​s′\nu\_{ss^{\prime}} and the solution bs,j​kb\_{s,jk}. Instead, on every iteration, we adjust the bs,j​kb\_{s,jk} to satisfy all required constraints, solve the linear system to find the Lagrange multipliers, and then use them in an eigenproblem to find the next bs,j​kb\_{s,jk}.

Here, this transformation is performed solely to obtain the Lagrange multipliers λi​j\lambda\_{ij} ([82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E82 "In A.4 Lagrange Multipliers Calculation ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) in diagonal form, which is necessary to find a stationary state solution of the time-dependent equation ([87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E87 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). For each solution of ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), the Lagrange multiplier matrix λ\lambda can be considered as a Hamiltonian of some quantum system. This can be viewed as up∗u\_{p\*} vectors evolving each with its own phase exp(−itλ[p]/ℏ)\exp\left(-it\lambda^{[p]}/\hbar\right). If we consider the operator up​ku\_{pk} as DD “wavefunctions” up∗u\_{p\*} of dimension nn, then each of them evolves with its own “energy” λ[p]\lambda^{[p]}. This represents the time evolution of the ground state solution of ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The difference from traditional quantum mechanics is that the ground state up​ku\_{pk} now contains multiple vectors, each evolving with its own exponent λ[p]\lambda^{[p]}. The density tensor corresponding to the ground state is

Unlike the density matrix of a traditional quantum system’s ground state, which does not depend on time, this density tensor has only the diagonal elements, p=p′p=p^{\prime}, that are independent of time. This explains why ([91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E91 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) is nonzero for a pure superstate Υ=|𝒰⟩​⟨𝒰|\Upsilon=\Ket{\mathcal{U}}\Bra{\mathcal{U}}, where 𝒰\mathcal{U} is the solution to ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

A [heat transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_equation#Statement_of_the_equation)-like equation can be obtained by removing the imaginary unit ii from ([87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E87 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), resulting in ϰ​∂𝒰/∂t=S​𝒰\varkappa\partial\mathcal{U}/\partial t=S\mathcal{U}. In this case, the solution ([97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E97 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) results in an exponentially growing or decaying up​k​(t)u\_{pk}(t).

The time evolution of a superposition of two solutions is more complicated compared to the Schrödinger equation. For the Schrödinger equation, a superposition of two eigenstates a​ψ[0]+b​ψ[1]a\psi^{[0]}+b\psi^{[1]} of a Hamiltonian time-evolves as aψ[0]exp(−itE0/ℏ)+bψ[1]exp(−itE1/ℏ)a\psi^{[0]}\exp\left(-itE\_{0}/\hbar\right)+b\psi^{[1]}\exp\left(-itE\_{1}/\hbar\right). At the same time, if we consider a superposition of two solutions a​uj​k[0]+b​uj​k[1]au^{[0]}\_{jk}+bu^{[1]}\_{jk} of ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), the result may not be unitary. The violation of unitarity resulting from such a superposition has deep physical significance. Such a superposition does not describe a physical state and, therefore, should not be considered. A proper generalization is the introduction of the density supermatrix Υ\Upsilon ([89](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E89 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), which describes a mixed type of state.

Another feature that may differ between wavefunctions and quantum channels is the state post-measurement destruction rules. In traditional quantum mechanics, the state |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} is destroyed (at least partially) after the measurement act ⟨ψ|R|ψ⟩\Braket{\psi|R|\psi}. In contrast, the measurement ⟨𝒰|R|𝒰⟩\Braket{\mathcal{U}|R|\mathcal{U}} involves a quantum channel 𝒰\mathcal{U} as the state. The post-measurement destruction rules for a quantum channel 𝒰\mathcal{U} remain an open question. It is possible that these rules differ between wavefunctions and quantum channels. A very important question is what the measurable unit is in quantum channel dynamics: whether it is a scalar or a Hermitian matrix? Since the corresponding algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) has eigenmatrices as its spectrum, rather than the usual eigenvalues (scalars), we are inclined to believe that the measurement unit is a Hermitian matrix. As the ground state energy of a quantum system can be obtained as a result of a single measurement act, a quantum channel single measurement could potentially provide the Hamiltonian λ[0]\lambda^{[0]} corresponding to the solution of ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) with the maximal fidelity.

For these reasons, we will leave a detailed consideration of the time-dependent equations ([87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E87 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([90](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E90 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) for future research and limit ourselves to the time evolution ([97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E97 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) of the ground state, which corresponds to each up∗u\_{p\*} vector evolving with its own “energy” λ[p]\lambda^{[p]}. The total fidelity is equal to the sum of all λ[p]\lambda^{[p]}, and the ground state is the state with the maximum total fidelity. The ground state solution corresponds to a unitary operator 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) that itself depends on time ([97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E97 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")).

children.heading: Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop

content.text: In this and previous works, we considered a [memoryless quantum channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_channel#Memoryless_quantum_channel) described by a set of Kraus operators BsB\_{s} or, in the simplest case where Ns=1N\_{s}=1, by a single unitary operator 𝒰\mathcal{U}. A question arises about how memory can be introduced into the model. Modeling a system with even a single bit of internal state is a daunting task, see Appendix H of [Malyshkin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib20), where we discuss the problem of modeling a [synchronous positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flip-flop_(electronics)#Classical_positive-edge-triggered_D_flip-flop) (D trigger) with ML. Any memory can be represented by a feedback loop, as seen in, for example, a D-trigger or a [recurrent neural network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network). The question is how to introduce memory into the quantum channel ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) described by an operator 𝒰\mathcal{U}? For pure states, the channel transforms an input state |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} into the output state |𝒰|ψ⟩\Ket{\mathcal{U}|\psi}. Let’s assume there is a feedback loop that requires some (but not all) components of the output state to be equal (within a phase) to the same components of the input state.

Here the {k}\{k\} denotes these selected “feedbacked” components. If {k}\{k\} is an empty set, we obtain the problem we considered in [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11). If {k}\{k\} includes all nn components — then ([99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3.E99 "In Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) becomes a regular eigenproblem with λ\lambda being exp⁡(i​ζ)\exp(i\zeta) (or ±1\pm 1 for an orthogonal uj​ku\_{jk}). In this case the problem does not have any input and the internal state can be represented as a superposition of nn eigenstates of eigenproblem ([99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3.E99 "In Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Now consider {k}\{k\} to be a subset of 0​…​n−10\dots n-1 indices with a total of nmn\_{m} elements. Then the problem ([99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3.E99 "In Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) represents an eigenvalue-like problem of dimension nmn\_{m}, i=0​…​nm−1i=0\dots n\_{m}-1, where an “eigenvector” |ψ[i]⟩\Ket{\psi^{[i]}} (there are nmn\_{m} total) has n−nmn-n\_{m} components set externally and nmn\_{m} components being an internal state. This “partial eigenvalue” ([99](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3.E99 "In Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) problem is a simple way to represent a quantum channel with an internal state (memory). A given state |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi} has n−nmn-n\_{m} free components (input) and nmn\_{m} components of the internal state. A change in the input components can potentially cause changes in the internal state. The study of unitary quantum channels with internal states is a subject for our future research.

A different application of these “feedbacked” states of a unitary operator relates to the problem of integer factorization. An integer can be encoded into a state |ψ⟩\Ket{\psi}, and the multiplication of the integer modulo NN by a number aa can be represented as a unitary transformation 𝒰\mathcal{U}.
