children.heading: Appendix D An estimate of computational complexity

content.text: The described class of algorithms solves QCQP problems that arise in the maximization of quadratic fidelity, subject to quadratic constraints on mapping operators (e.g., unitarity). This problem is equivalent to an algebraic problem; for example, in the case of unitary learning, it corresponds to the algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) originally introduced in [Malyshkin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib20). This represents the simplest problem of this type. In the general case, this is a new algebraic problem of dimension Ns​D​nN\_{s}Dn. It can be solved numerically using an iterative algorithm that, on each iteration, replaces NcN\_{c} quadratic constraints with Nc−1N\_{c}-1 homogeneous linear constraints and a single quadratic constraint ([26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E26 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), referred to as a simplified (partial) constraint, see Appendix [A.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS5 "A.5 Convergence-Helper Linear Constraints ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") above. Since a QCQP problem with a single quadratic constraint is equivalent to an eigenvalue problem, a regular eigenvalue problem solver is applied to a problem of dimension NV=Ns​D​n−Nc+1N\_{V}=N\_{s}Dn-N\_{c}+1, this is step [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.I2.i1 "item 1 ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") of the algorithm. As discussed in Appendix B of [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11), this is the most computationally intensive step. Its computational complexity in the unitary learning case (D=nD=n, Ns=1N\_{s}=1) involves solving an eigenproblem with a matrix of dimension NV=n2−n⁡(n+1)/2+1N\_{V}=n^{2}-n(n+1)/2+1. This complexity can be estimated as O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) when using a specialized solver optimized to find only the maximal eigenvalue and O⁡(n6)O(n^{6}) when using a general-purpose solver. Our current implementation [Malyshkin 2014](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib19) uses a general-purpose eigenvalue solver.

Let us compare the computational complexity of this “algebraic” algorithm with that of the “mathematical analysis” ones: second-order Newton’s method and first-order gradient method. A unitary matrix of dimension nn can be completely parametrized with N=n⁡(n+1)/2N=n(n+1)/2 parameters. There are nn fewer parameters if we do not need unmeasurable phases. The number of parameters is always greater than or equal to n⁡(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2 (e.g., Euler angles), see ([97](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E97 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), which gives a time-dependent ground state unitary operator 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) such that, at every time moment tt, the matrix 𝒰\mathcal{U} gives the maximal value of fidelity ℱ\mathcal{F} ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). The complexity of the classical Newton’s method for nonlinear systems of NN equations is O⁡(Ni​t​N3)O(N\_{it}N^{3}), as a linear system needs to be solved at each iteration. Some tricks, such as updating the Jacobian only once every mm iterations, can reduce the complexity to O⁡(Ni​t​N2+Ni​t​N3/m)O(N\_{it}N^{2}+N\_{it}N^{3}/m). Since the number of iterations, Ni​tN\_{it}, for Newton’s method is often independent of NN, the practical complexity of the Newton’s method algorithm can be estimated to lie between O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) and O⁡(n6)O(n^{6}),77 7 If all MM observations are not combined into a single entity, such as Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}}, then the complexity may range between O⁡(M​n4)O(Mn^{4}) and O⁡(M​n6)O(Mn^{6}), which significantly worsens the result. depending on the Jacobian updating strategy. While the computational complexity of the proposed algebraic algorithm is comparable to that of the second-order Newton’s method, using the generalized eigenvalue problem as the algorithm’s building block offers the advantage of obtaining multiple solution candidates (eigenvectors). Numerical experiments[Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) demonstrate that this significantly increases the chances of finding the global maximum.

The computational complexity of the gradient method in the general case is O⁡(Ni​t​M​N)O(N\_{it}MN). If the MM-sum can be factored out from the objective functional (e.g., into a form like ([27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E27 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"))), the complexity reduces to O⁡(Ni​t​N2)=O⁡(Ni​t​n4)O(N\_{it}N^{2})=O(N\_{it}n^{4}). However, in the gradient method, the number of iterations Ni​tN\_{it} is not guaranteed to be small, nor is the algorithm guaranteed to converge, especially for a global optimization problem that is nonconvex, with local extrema and multiple saddle points.

The developed algorithm exhibits computational complexity on par with second-order Newton’s method and higher than that of the first-order gradient method. Its main feature is the algebraic approach, which enables the construction of a globally converging algorithm. While we lack a formal proof of its convergence, among millions of test runs, only a few failed to converge to the global maximum. In this work, we aimed to address a practical problem that can be validated using a classical computer. Consider a scenario where we have input data (e.g., in the form of files on disk), and we seek to recover the corresponding quantum mapping. This problem frequently arises in Machine Learning for large dimensions, as discussed in [Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2) and over 1,000 subsequent papers citing it. In the notations of the submitted paper, typical dimensions of the ML problem are Ns=1N\_{s}=1 and D=n∼103D=n\sim 10^{3} or greater. The solution involves a form of unitary parametrization[Raza 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib5), such as representing the unitary as a series of elementary rotations (e.g., Euler angles) and employing a gradient-based optimization method. The resulting solution is obtained through this process, but there is no guarantee that it corresponds to the global maximum. Our primary focus was on developing an algorithm capable of providing the global maximum solution. For this reason we considered an exact unitary mapping and aimed to recover it from a sample, this is why we did not include noise or other common features in our study. This is a highly challenging nonconvex problem, as the number of parameters grows quadratically with nn [Andersson et al. 2007](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib44). To the best of our knowledge, practical solutions are feasible only for small nn (fewer than a dozen) or under specific setups [Schäfers et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib38); [Ahmed et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib18); [Wang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib14). In our numerical experiments for unitary learning, the problem’s dimensionality appears to be constrained solely by computational complexity. At each iteration step, an eigenvalue problem of dimension NV=n2−n⁡(n+1)/2+1N\_{V}=n^{2}-n(n+1)/2+1 must be solved, with only the eigenstate corresponding to the largest eigenvalue being required. Given the extensive global effort devoted to developing efficient numerical solvers for eigenproblems, we anticipate that the dimensionality of the problem can be significantly increased. Currently, however, we lack access to hardware capable of solving eigenproblems for matrices larger than dimension 1000. Our original goal was to push the problem’s dimensionality to a point where exact recovery of orthogonal (real unitary) matrices would become infeasible. However, computational limits were encountered first. In our experiments, we tested the exact recovery of thousands of randomly generated orthogonal matrices with dimensions under 50 (corresponding to an eigenproblem size of 1226). The ability to find the global maximum remains the algorithm’s most significant feature.

The computational complexity of constructing the tensor Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} ([19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E19 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) was insignificant for the pure state unitary mapping ([1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E1 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) discussed in [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11). However, for the unitary mapping ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) of mixed states ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) considered in the present work, obtaining the fidelity in quadratic form requires transforming the mapping to a density matrix square root mapping ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). This transformation may significantly increase the computational complexity of calculating Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} ([30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E30 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Using an eigenvalue problem to calculate the square root of a matrix would require solving MM eigenproblems with the matrices ρ\rho and ϱ\varrho, each of dimension nn, resulting in a complexity of the order O⁡(M​n3)O(Mn^{3}). This cannot be reduced as in the QCQP case above, where only a single eigenvector was needed. For the density matrix square root, we need all eigenvectors, and the calculation of ([30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E30 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) probably cannot be done any better than O⁡(M​n3)O(Mn^{3}). The factor before that can, however, be reduced. When the number of observations MM is large, instead of using the regular method of calculating the matrix square root by solving an eigenproblem (as in ([71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E71 "In A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E78 "In A.3 An Adjustment of a Quantum Channel to Preserve the Trace ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) above), one can apply alternative methods to compute the square root of a positively definite Hermitian matrix without solving an eigenproblem [Björck 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib45); [Higham 1986](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib46). These approaches, like the eigenvalue problem, have a dominant complexity of O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) for the square root computation. However, in practice, it can significantly improve computational efficiency when creating the mapping ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) from the original data ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Despite the complexity of calculating Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} for a large MM, this creates no difficulty in applications since the calculations are similar to those used, for example, in covariance matrix computation. Each component of the tensor is a sum over all MM observations, and this task can be trivially parallelized.

The general Kraus case, Ns>1N\_{s}>1, is significantly more difficult, since the fidelity ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), as a quadratic form, can only be obtained as an approximation. However, once the approximation is obtained, in the general case, it requires solving an eigenproblem of dimension NV=Ns​D​n−Nc+1N\_{V}=N\_{s}Dn-N\_{c}+1 at each iteration (step [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.I2.i1 "item 1 ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") of the algorithm), with only a single eigenvector corresponding to the maximal eigenvalue being needed. For a general quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), we were not able to construct a converging algorithm, not to mention the increased computational complexity (eigenvalue problem dimension is increased in Kraus rank times). However, if we limit ourselves to mixed-unitary channels ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), then this type of quantum channel can be reconstructed as a hierarchy of unitary operators. Computationally, the problem in Section [IV](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4 "IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") is much simpler than a general quantum channel reconstruction. Instead of dealing with a single complicated general quantum channel problem, the problem of unitary mapping needs to be solved several times. Numerically, we were able to obtain a hierarchy of no more than 77 operators, which is probably due to the suboptimal algorithm for constraint conflict resolution used in Appendix [A.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS2 "A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). The result is a mixed unitary channel ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). However, contrary to the Ns=1N\_{s}=1 case, for Ns>1N\_{s}>1, this is only an approximation, since we were not able to represent the proper fidelity ([11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E11 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) as the quadratic form of Eq. ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) in Kraus operators BsB\_{s} when Ns>1N\_{s}>1.

## I Introduction

The form of knowledge representation stands out as a crucial and distinctive feature in any approach to Machine Learning (ML). The utilization of unitary operators for knowledge representation has garnered increasing attention recently[Bisio et al. 2010](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib1); [Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2); [Hyland and Rätsch 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib3). In nature most of dynamic equations are equivalent to a sequence of infinitesimal unitary transformations: Newton, Maxwell, Schrödinger equations. This inherent connection with unitary transformations makes it particularly appealing to represent knowledge in this form. Most of the existing works consider algorithms that take wavefunction as input and construct a unitary operator providing a high value of mapping fidelity[Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2); [Hyland and Rätsch 2017](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib3); [Lloyd and Maity 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib4); they are mostly different in parametrization of unitary operator [Raza 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib5) and optimization details. Such a pure state to pure state mapping is a limited form of quantum evolution. There are a few works[Pai et al. 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib6); [Huang et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib7); [González et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib8); [Yu et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib9) that consider unitary learning with density matrix input. Real systems probability should be described by a mixed state (density matrix) what allows to distinguish probabilistic mixture of states and their superposition. There are two sources of mixed states: 1. The input data itself can be in mixed state. 2. ​I​N→​O​U​T\emph{IN}\to\emph{OUT} mapping of a general quantum channel can transform a pure state input into a mixed state output. Unitary mapping is a simple example of a quantum channel converting a pure state into a pure state.

​I​N→​O​U​T\emph{IN}\to\emph{OUT}

In our previous works[Malyshkin 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib10); [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11) the quantum mechanics inverse problem of optimal unitary mapping of pure states was converted to a [QCQP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratically_constrained_quadratic_program) (Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program) problem, a novel algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) was formulated, and an efficient iterative global optimization algorithm was developed. This algorithm can be applied to quantum inverse problems, variational quantum algorithms [Cerezo et al. 2021](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib12); [Park and Killoran 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib13); [Wang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib14) with a cost function in the form C⁡(θ)=Tr​O​𝒰​(θ)​ρ0​𝒰†​(θ)C(\theta)=\mathrm{Tr}\,O\mathcal{U}(\theta)\rho\_{0}\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}(\theta), quantum tomography[D’Ariano et al. 2003](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib15); [Lvovsky and Raymer 2009](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib16); [Torlai et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib17); [Ahmed et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib18), various classical problems, and many others. We do not have a formal proof of the developed algorithm’s convergence, but among the millions of test runs, only a few did not converge to the global maximum. This could possibly be caused by numerical instability. In the current work, we generalize our algorithm to mixed states and further extend it to quantum channels. This generalization is possible as long as the total fidelity can be represented as a quadratic form on quantum channel mapping operators.

C⁡(θ)=Tr​O​𝒰​(θ)​ρ0​𝒰†​(θ)C(\theta)=\mathrm{Tr}\,O\mathcal{U}(\theta)\rho_{0}\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}(\theta)

In the case of unitary mapping (D=nD=n, Ns=1N\_{s}=1) of mixed states there are several good choices for fidelity, for example a quantum channel mapping the square root of density matrix ρ→ϱ\sqrt{\rho}\to\sqrt{\varrho} with a unitary operator ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), it provides the exact fidelity as a quadratic form. Together with the available iterative algorithm, this problem may be considered mostly solved.

In the case of a general quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) constructing fidelity as the quadratic form of Eq. ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) on quantum channel mapping operators can be challenging. We have developed several approximations that can be used with the iterative algorithm and have constructed a hierarchy of mapping operators ([52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E52 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) as a mixed unitary channel. A demonstration of several approximations is presented in Section [IV.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.SS1 "IV.1 A Demonstration of Constructed Hierarchy of Operators ‣ IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). The problem of finding a good quadratic (on mapping operators) fidelity for Kraus rank Ns>1N\_{s}>1 quantum channels requires more research and is related to a physical meaning of quantum channel mapping. Even when fidelity is expressed as the quadratic form of Eq. ([16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E16 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), we currently only have a numerical algorithm to approximate the data using a mixed unitary channel. A general reconstruction of quantum channels is not yet available.

The paper is organized as follows. After formulating the problem, the unitary mapping of mixed states is considered in Section [III](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3 "III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning"). Section [IV](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4 "IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") focuses on the construction of a hierarchy of unitary operators. In the conclusion, we discuss the results obtained for the problem of quantum channel reconstruction. Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1 "Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") provides a detailed description of the numerical solution that uses algebraic techniques. Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2 "Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") presents a generalization of the novel algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) to the nonstationary case and introduces a time-dependent Schrödinger-like equation for unitary operator dynamics ([87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A2.E87 "In Appendix B A Time-Dependent Schrödinger-like Equation ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A3 "Appendix C Parametrizing states with memory using a feedback loop ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") explores potential generalizations to states with memory, while Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A4 "Appendix D An estimate of computational complexity ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") estimates the algorithm’s computational complexity.

This paper is accompanied by a software which [is available](http://www.ioffe.ru/LNEPS/malyshkin/code_polynomials_quadratures.zip) from Ref. [Malyshkin 2014](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib19); all references to code in the paper correspond to this software.

## Appendix D An estimate of computational complexity

The described class of algorithms solves QCQP problems that arise in the maximization of quadratic fidelity, subject to quadratic constraints on mapping operators (e.g., unitarity). This problem is equivalent to an algebraic problem; for example, in the case of unitary learning, it corresponds to the algebraic problem ([43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E43 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) originally introduced in [Malyshkin 2019](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib20). This represents the simplest problem of this type. In the general case, this is a new algebraic problem of dimension Ns​D​nN\_{s}Dn. It can be solved numerically using an iterative algorithm that, on each iteration, replaces NcN\_{c} quadratic constraints with Nc−1N\_{c}-1 homogeneous linear constraints and a single quadratic constraint ([26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E26 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), referred to as a simplified (partial) constraint, see Appendix [A.5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.SS5 "A.5 Convergence-Helper Linear Constraints ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") above. Since a QCQP problem with a single quadratic constraint is equivalent to an eigenvalue problem, a regular eigenvalue problem solver is applied to a problem of dimension NV=Ns​D​n−Nc+1N\_{V}=N\_{s}Dn-N\_{c}+1, this is step [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.I2.i1 "item 1 ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") of the algorithm. As discussed in Appendix B of [Belov and Malyshkin 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib11), this is the most computationally intensive step. Its computational complexity in the unitary learning case (D=nD=n, Ns=1N\_{s}=1) involves solving an eigenproblem with a matrix of dimension NV=n2−n⁡(n+1)/2+1N\_{V}=n^{2}-n(n+1)/2+1. This complexity can be estimated as O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) when using a specialized solver optimized to find only the maximal eigenvalue and O⁡(n6)O(n^{6}) when using a general-purpose solver. The developed algorithm exhibits computational complexity on par with second-order Newton’s method and higher than that of the first-order gradient method. Its main feature is the algebraic approach, which enables the construction of a globally converging algorithm. While we lack a formal proof of its convergence, among millions of test runs, only a few failed to converge to the global maximum. In this work, we aimed to address a practical problem that can be validated using a classical computer. Consider a scenario where we have input data (e.g., in the form of files on disk), and we seek to recover the corresponding quantum mapping. This problem frequently arises in Machine Learning for large dimensions, as discussed in [Arjovsky et al. 2016](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib2) and over 1,000 subsequent papers citing it. In the notations of the submitted paper, typical dimensions of the ML problem are Ns=1N\_{s}=1 and D=n∼103D=n\sim 10^{3} or greater. The solution involves a form of unitary parametrization[Raza 2020](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib5), such as representing the unitary as a series of elementary rotations (e.g., Euler angles) and employing a gradient-based optimization method. The resulting solution is obtained through this process, but there is no guarantee that it corresponds to the global maximum. Our primary focus was on developing an algorithm capable of providing the global maximum solution. For this reason we considered an exact unitary mapping and aimed to recover it from a sample, this is why we did not include noise or other common features in our study. This is a highly challenging nonconvex problem, as the number of parameters grows quadratically with nn [Andersson et al. 2007](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib44). To the best of our knowledge, practical solutions are feasible only for small nn (fewer than a dozen) or under specific setups [Schäfers et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib38); [Ahmed et al. 2023](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib18); [Wang et al. 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib14). In our numerical experiments for unitary learning, the problem’s dimensionality appears to be constrained solely by computational complexity. At each iteration step, an eigenvalue problem of dimension NV=n2−n⁡(n+1)/2+1N\_{V}=n^{2}-n(n+1)/2+1 must be solved, with only the eigenstate corresponding to the largest eigenvalue being required. Given the extensive global effort devoted to developing efficient numerical solvers for eigenproblems, we anticipate that the dimensionality of the problem can be significantly increased. Currently, however, we lack access to hardware capable of solving eigenproblems for matrices larger than dimension 1000. Our original goal was to push the problem’s dimensionality to a point where exact recovery of orthogonal (real unitary) matrices would become infeasible. However, computational limits were encountered first. In our experiments, we tested the exact recovery of thousands of randomly generated orthogonal matrices with dimensions under 50 (corresponding to an eigenproblem size of 1226). The ability to find the global maximum remains the algorithm’s most significant feature.

However, for the unitary mapping ([3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E3 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) of mixed states ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) considered in the present work, obtaining the fidelity in quadratic form requires transforming the mapping to a density matrix square root mapping ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). This transformation may significantly increase the computational complexity of calculating Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} ([30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E30 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Using an eigenvalue problem to calculate the square root of a matrix would require solving MM eigenproblems with the matrices ρ\rho and ϱ\varrho, each of dimension nn, resulting in a complexity of the order O⁡(M​n3)O(Mn^{3}). This cannot be reduced as in the QCQP case above, where only a single eigenvector was needed. For the density matrix square root, we need all eigenvectors, and the calculation of ([30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E30 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) probably cannot be done any better than O⁡(M​n3)O(Mn^{3}). The factor before that can, however, be reduced. When the number of observations MM is large, instead of using the regular method of calculating the matrix square root by solving an eigenproblem (as in ([71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E71 "In A.2 An Adjustment of Operators to Orthogonal ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) and ([78](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.E78 "In A.3 An Adjustment of a Quantum Channel to Preserve the Trace ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) above), one can apply alternative methods to compute the square root of a positively definite Hermitian matrix without solving an eigenproblem [Björck 2024](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib45); [Higham 1986](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#bib.bib46). These approaches, like the eigenvalue problem, have a dominant complexity of O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) for the square root computation. However, in practice, it can significantly improve computational efficiency when creating the mapping ([29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S3.E29 "In III A Unitary Mapping of Mixed States ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")) from the original data ([7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E7 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")). Despite the complexity of calculating Sj​k;j′​k′S\_{jk;j^{\prime}k^{\prime}} for a large MM, this creates no difficulty in applications since the calculations are similar to those used, for example, in covariance matrix computation. Each component of the tensor is a sum over all MM observations, and this task can be trivially parallelized.

However, once the approximation is obtained, in the general case, it requires solving an eigenproblem of dimension NV=Ns​D​n−Nc+1N\_{V}=N\_{s}Dn-N\_{c}+1 at each iteration (step [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#A1.I2.i1 "item 1 ‣ Appendix A Numerical Solution ‣ Quantum Channel Learning") of the algorithm), with only a single eigenvector corresponding to the maximal eigenvalue being needed. For a general quantum channel ([4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S2.E4 "In II Formulation of the Problem ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), we were not able to construct a converging algorithm, not to mention the increased computational complexity (eigenvalue problem dimension is increased in Kraus rank times). However, if we limit ourselves to mixed-unitary channels ([36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2407.04406#S4.E36 "In IV A Hierarchy of Unitary Operators ‣ Quantum Channel Learning")), then this type of quantum channel can be reconstructed as a hierarchy of unitary operators. Instead of dealing with a single complicated general quantum channel problem, the problem of unitary mapping needs to be solved several times.
